source_text: Πρὸς δὲ τοῖς εἰρημένοις πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπον τὴν μὲν ἀρετὴν καὶ τὴν κακίαν μηδὲ νοηθῆναι δύνασθαι χωρὶς ἐπὶ τῆς ψυχῆς (ἀνθρώπου γὰρ ἀρετὰς εἶναι γινώσκομεν τὰς ἀρετάς, ὡσπεροῦν καὶ τὴν ταύταις ἀντικειμένην κακίαν οὐ ψυχῆς κεχωρισμένης τοῦ σώματος καὶ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν οὔσης), τὴν δ᾿ ἐπὶ τούτοις τιμὴν ἢ τιμωρίαν ἐπὶ μόνης φέρεσθαι τῆς ψυχῆς; Ἢ πῶς ἄν τις καὶ νοήσειεν ἐπὶ ψυχῆς μόνης ἀνδρείαν ἢ καρτερίαν, οὐκ ἐχούσης οὐ θανάτου φόβον, οὐ τραύματος οὐ πηρώσεως οὐ ζημίας οὐκ αἰκίας, οὐ τῶν ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀλγημάτων ἢ τῆς ἐκ τούτων κακοπαθείας; Πῶς δὲ ἐγκράτειαν καὶ σωφροσύνην, οὐδεμιᾶς ἑλκούσης αὐτὴν ἐπιθυμίας πρὸς τροφὴν ἢ μῖξιν ἢ τὰς ἄλλας ἡδονάς τε καὶ τέρψεις, οὐδ᾿ ἄλλου τινὸς οὔτ᾿ ἔσωθεν ἐνοχλοῦντος οὔτ᾿ ἔξωθεν ἐρεθίζοντος; Πῶς δὲ φρόνησιν, οὐχ ὑποκειμένων αὐτῇ πρακτέων καὶ μὴ πρακτέων, οὔθ᾿ αἱρετῶν καὶ φευκτῶν, μᾶλλον δὲ μηδεμιᾶς ἐνούσης αὐτῇ κινήσεως τὸ παράπαν ἢ φυσικῆς ὁρμῆς ἐπί τι τῶν πρακτέων; Ποῦ δὲ ὅλως ψυχαῖς ἡ πρὸς ἀλλήλας δικαιοσύνη προσφυὴς ἢ πρὸς ἄλλο τι τῶν ὁμογενῶν ἢ ἑτερογενῶν, οὐκ ἐχούσαις οὔτε πόθεν οὔτε δι᾿ ὧν οὔτε πῶς ἀπονείμωσι τὸ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν ἢ κατ᾿ ἀναλογίαν ἴσον, ἐξῃρημένης τῆς εἰς θεὸν τιμῆς, οὐδ᾿ ἄλλως ἐχούσαις ὁρμὴν ἢ κίνησιν πρὸς χρῆσιν ἰδίων ἢ πρὸς ἀποχὴν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων, τῆς μὲν χρήσεως τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἢ τῆς ἀποχῆς ἐπὶ τῶν χρῆσθαι πεφυκότων θεωρουμένης, τῆς δὲ ψυχῆς μήτε δεομένης τινὸς μήτε χρῆσθαί τισιν ἤ τινι πεφυκυίας, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μήτε τῆς λεγομένης ἰδιοπραγίας τῶν μερῶν ἐπὶ τῆς οὕτως ἐχούσης ψυχῆς εὑρεθῆναι δυναμένης;
thought_title: Virtues and vices cannot belong to the soul alone
orientation: Athenagoras is arguing that if virtues and vices cannot even be conceived apart from the body, then honor and punishment for them cannot fall on the soul alone.
pass_a_gloss: And in addition to the things said, how is it not absurd that virtue and vice cannot even be conceived separately in the case of the soul (for we know that the virtues are virtues of a human being, just as also the vice opposed to these is not of a soul separated from the body and existing by itself), but that the honor or punishment for these is borne upon the soul alone? Or how would anyone even conceive courage or endurance in the case of the soul alone, [the soul] having no fear of death, no [fear] of wound, no [fear] of mutilation, no [fear] of loss, no [fear] of outrage, no [fear] of the pains upon these or of the suffering from these? And how [would anyone conceive] self-control and temperance, [with] no desire drawing it toward food or intercourse or the other pleasures and delights, and no other thing either from within troubling [it] or from without provoking [it]? And how [would anyone conceive] prudence, [with] things to be done and not to be done not being set before it, nor things to be chosen and things to be avoided, and rather [with] no movement at all being in it or natural impulse toward any of the things to be done? And where in general is justice toward one another natural to souls, or toward any other thing of the same kind or of a different kind, [souls] having neither whence nor through what nor how they might assign the equal according to worth or according to proportion, the honor toward God being excepted, nor otherwise having impulse or movement toward use of their own things or toward abstention from the things of others, the use of the things according to nature or the abstention being observed in the case of the things naturally able to use, but the soul neither needing anything nor naturally able to use any things or any thing, and because of this the so-called proper activity of the parts not being able to be found in the case of the soul being in this condition?

choices.why: The phrase is technical in Greek philosophy, referring to each part doing its own work; rendering it literally preserves the technical sense Athenagoras invokes.

choices.english: is borne upon the soul alone
choices.why: The passive of φέρω with ἐπί suggests the honor or punishment being carried or imposed upon the soul; 'borne upon' keeps the passive force and the sense of imposition.
rejected: is assigned to the soul alone

choices.why: The adjective means 'grown upon' or 'attached by nature'; 'natural to' captures the sense that justice belongs to souls by their nature, which is exactly what Athenagoras denies.

choices.english: the honor toward God being excepted
choices.why: The genitive absolute marks an exception; 'being excepted' preserves the grammatical structure and the logical point that honor to God is the one thing souls can render.
rejected: apart from the honor to God

choices.why: The noun denotes the experience of hardship or distress; 'suffering' is the plain English equivalent and avoids the archaic 'affliction.'

pass_b_english: In addition to what has already been said, is it not absurd to hold that virtue and vice cannot even be conceived in the soul alone—since we recognize that the virtues are virtues of a human being, just as the vice opposed to them is not that of a soul separated from the body and existing by itself—yet the honor or punishment for these is borne upon the soul alone?

How could anyone even conceive of courage or endurance in a soul by itself? It has no fear of death, wound, mutilation, loss, or outrage, nor of the pains that come from these or the suffering they cause.

How could self-control and temperance exist in it, when no desire draws it toward food or sexual union or the other pleasures and delights, and nothing else troubles it from within or provokes it from without?

How could prudence exist in it, when there are no things to be done or not done, no things to be chosen or avoided, laid before it—indeed, when it has no movement at all or natural impulse toward any of the things to be done?

And where at all is justice between souls natural to them, or justice toward anything else of the same kind or of a different kind, when they have no source, no means, and no manner by which to assign what is equal according to worth or proportion—the honor toward God being excepted—and when they have no impulse or movement either to use what is their own or to abstain from what belongs to others?

For the use of natural things, or abstinence from them, belongs to beings made by nature to use them; but the soul needs nothing and is not naturally suited to use anything or anyone, and for this reason the so-called proper activity of the parts cannot be found in a soul that is in such a condition.

problems.why: Greek means 'in the soul alone/without the body', not 'apart from the soul'
problems.ruling: χωρὶς ἐπὶ τῆς ψυχῆς means 'apart from the soul' as in 'on the soul alone'; English reverses the argument's logic.

edits.new: virtue and vice cannot even be conceived in the soul alone

problems.quote: the vice opposed to them belongs not to a soul separated from the body and existing by itself
problems.source_quote: οὐ ψυχῆς κεχωρισμένης τοῦ σώματος καὶ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν οὔσης
problems.why: English says vice 'belongs not to' separated soul, but Greek says it IS of separated soul; negation misplaced.
problems.fix: just as the vice opposed to them belongs to a soul separated from the body and existing by itself
problems.ruling: Greek says virtues are recognized as human virtues, 'just as vice IS of a separated soul' (ὡσπεροῦν...οὐ ψυχῆς). English 'belongs not to' reverses the negation, misreading the clause.

problems.ruling: Greek genitive absolutes (θεωρουμένης, δεομένης, πεφυκυίας) are subordinate; English makes them independent main clauses, breaking sentence structure.

fixed: The first problem was real: the English omitted the negative 'not' before 'of a soul separated', reversing the meaning. Fixed by changing 'belongs to a soul' to 'is not that of a soul'.

The second problem was real: the English turned the genitive absolute into a main clause, breaking the syntax. Fixed by changing 'For the use' to 'since the use' and removing the period, making it a subordinate clause.
